A hermit is a person who deliberately chooses to live alone, cut off from other people and from mainstream society. The key word here is deliberately — a hermit is not lonely by accident or by force. It is a conscious, personal choice. They pull away from the world, seek solitude, and prefer their own company (or no company at all) over the company of others.

Think of it this way: most people live surrounded by family, neighbours, colleagues, and friends. A hermit does the opposite. They step away from all of that.
The Two Main Worlds of This Word

The word "hermit" lives in two worlds — a traditional/religious one, and a modern/everyday one.

1. The Religious or Spiritual Hermit

This is the original and deeper meaning. In many religious traditions — particularly Christianity, Buddhism, and Hinduism — some deeply devoted individuals chose to leave society entirely to focus on prayer, meditation, and spiritual growth. They believed that the noise, distractions, and temptations of ordinary social life pulled them away from their spiritual goals. So they retreated.

These hermits typically lived in:

  • Deserts (the famous "Desert Fathers" of early Christianity lived in the Egyptian desert)
  • Caves
  • Dense forests
  • Remote mountains
  • Small, isolated huts or cells

They lived with almost nothing — very simple food, no luxuries, minimal possessions. The point wasn't to be miserable; it was to strip life down to what they felt truly mattered: their inner, spiritual life. Many became deeply respected as holy or wise figures, and people would sometimes travel great distances just to seek their advice.

2. The Modern or Informal Hermit

In everyday modern language, "hermit" has a broader, looser meaning. It refers to any person who avoids social contact and lives in isolation, whether for religious reasons or not. You do not need to be spiritual or live in a cave to be called a hermit today.

Someone might be called a hermit if they:

  • Rarely leave their home
  • Avoid parties, gatherings, or social events
  • Have little to no contact with friends, family, or neighbours
  • live in a very remote, faraway place by choice

In this modern sense, the word is often used informally and even humorously. For example, if your friend never comes out and always stays home, you might joke, "Oh, he's turned into a complete hermit!" It is not always meant as a serious insult — it can be light-hearted.
What Makes Someone a Hermit vs. Just a Shy Person?

This is an important distinction. A shy or introverted person may dislike crowds or feel drained by socialising, but they still live a normal life within society. A hermit takes it to a much further extreme — they actively withdraw from society as a whole, not just from big social events. It is a matter of degree and commitment. Shyness is a personality trait; hermitery (living as a hermit) is a lifestyle choice.
The Qualities We Associate with a Hermit

When you picture a hermit, certain qualities typically come to mind:

  • Solitude: They spend most or all of their time alone.
  • Simplicity: They tend to live simply, without many possessions or luxuries.
  • Self-sufficiency: They rely on themselves, not on a community, for their needs.
  • Withdrawal: They have deliberately turned away from society, its norms, noise, and demands.
  • Contemplation: Many (especially in the religious sense) spend a great deal of time thinking deeply, praying, or reflecting.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples that show the word used naturally, ranging from serious to casual:

  • "The old hermit lived alone in the mountains for thirty years, speaking to almost no one."
  • "After retiring, he became something of a hermit, rarely leaving his countryside cottage."
  • "She joked that she had become a hermit during the winter, barely stepping outside for weeks."
  • "The spiritual hermit was known for his wisdom, and travellers sought him for guidance."
  • "Don't be such a hermit — come out with us tonight!"

• Recluse — very close in meaning to hermit; a person who lives a withdrawn, solitary life. Often used in modern, non-religious contexts. (e.g., "She was a recluse who never answered the door.")
  • Solitary — can be used as a noun or adjective for someone who lives alone or prefers to be alone.
  • Ascetic — someone who gives up pleasures and comforts, often for religious reasons; many hermits were also ascetics, but the words are not the same — an ascetic focuses on self-denial, while a hermit focuses on isolation.
A Fun Fact Worth Knowing: The Hermit Crab

The animal called the hermit crab gets its name from this very word. A hermit crab lives alone inside a borrowed shell, carrying its solitary home wherever it goes — just like a hermit retreating into their own private world, separate from others. It is a fitting name.

If you had to boil it down to a single sentence:

A hermit is someone who chooses to live alone and apart from society — whether for spiritual, personal, or philosophical reasons — withdrawing from the world in favour of solitude.
